summary: Albertans vote Monday on whether to stay in Canada, Ontario will import U.S. power this winter, and Anthropic picks Nova Scotia for its first Canadian data centre.
body: Alberta votes tomorrow. Polls are open Monday from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m. Alberta time, and Question 10, on whether to stay in Canada or hold a second, binding vote on leaving, will be counted first, with early results expected Monday night [^1]. Ballots are counted by hand; results on the other nine questions, on topics such as immigration and the constitution, should come by Wednesday [^1]. Elections Alberta said more than 700,000 people had voted at advance polls by Saturday, and total ballots passed one million on Thursday [^2][^3]. A Leger online poll taken Oct. 14 to 16 found 74% planned to vote to remain and 21% to start the separation process [^4]. Polls are not results, so Monday night is what counts.

Closer to home: Ontario's grid operator (the IESO) has signed a six-month deal, starting Nov. 1, to import 600 megawatts of power from a U.S. company this winter [^5]. Ontario normally sells power to Michigan, New York and Minnesota, and in August Premier Doug Ford said he was willing to cut off electricity to the U.S. in the trade war [^5]. The IESO calls the deal normal planning for winter demand and maintenance; the Toronto Sun reports it will cover shortfalls while the Pickering nuclear plant is refurbished [^5][^6]. The cost was not disclosed [^6].

In Nova Scotia, Anthropic, the U.S. company that makes the Claude AI models, signed a 20-year lease at a planned data centre at Point Tupper in Cape Breton. Developer EverWind says it will invest $8 billion in the campus and $2 billion in wind farms; the first phase is due in late 2027 [^7][^8]. Disclosure: Anthropic makes the AI that writes this brief.

On the economy, Statistics Canada releases September inflation on Monday. Economists polled by Reuters expect 3.2%, up from 3.0% in August, ahead of the Bank of Canada's Oct. 28 rate decision; the bank's rate has been 2.25% for nearly a year [^9].
differences: People read the Ontario power deal differently. The IESO says it is routine and that Ontario exported about seven times more power than it imported in 2025 [^5]. Critics, including Environmental Defence and the Ontario Clean Air Alliance, call it "ironic" given Ford's threats and say more clean power should have been built [^5][^6]. In Nova Scotia, the NDP asks how promises to protect ratepayers will be enforced; the premier says existing approvals are enough [^7].
